captures.text: L5 PracticalFLOATYThe 'bone' inside a cuttlefish is called the cuttlebone. Despite the name, it is not a bone at all. It is actually the cuttlefish’s internal shell, made mostly of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) arranged in a very light, porous structure.Inside the cuttlebone are thousands of tiny chambers separated by thin walls. A cuttlefish can control how much liquid and gas are inside these chambers, allowing it to adjust its buoyancy. By changing the pressure inside the cuttlebone, the animal can rise or sink in the water without swimming, much like a submarine using ballast tanks.Your job is to calculate the density of a dry cuttlebone.Instructions1) Using a 50 cm³ measuring cylinder and some distilled water, measure the volume of your cuttlebone.Hint: work quickly, as the cuttlebone will begin to absorb water. You can hold it just below the water level with a stirring rod.ENTER THE VOLUME BELOW2) Dry the cuttlebone with blue roll, then crush it using a pestle and mortar.3) React it with 114 cm³ of 2 mol/dm³ HCl in a beaker. You will need to stir this well to ensure the acid reacts fully with the crushed cuttlebone.Hint: it might be quite time efficient for one of you to skip ahead to step 5 to start getting the titration ready to go.4) Transfer the reaction mixture to a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and fill to the line with distilled water.Hint: make sure all of the mixture is transferred into the volumetric flask.5) Fill the burette with 1 mol/dm³ NaOH. Take a 25 cm³ sample of the solution containing the cuttlebone reaction mixture and add a few drops of phenolphthalein.6) Titrate the solution (if you have not done a titration before, ask the supervising teacher for help).7) Repeat the titration until you obtain consistent results (or run out of time). Calculate the average titration result (the mean titre).ENTER THE MEAN TITRE BELOW8) Calculate the moles of NaOH used in the titration.NaOH reacts with HCl as follows:NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)9) Calculate the moles of HCl in 25 cm³ of solution.10) Calculate the moles of HCl in 250 cm³ of solution.11) Calculate the moles of HCl that reacted with the cuttlebone.ENTER THE MOLES OF HCl BELOWCalcium carbonate reacts as follows:CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)12) Calculate the moles of CaCO₃ in the cuttlebone.13) Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ in the cuttlebone.14) Calculate the density of the cuttlebone.ENTER THE DENSITY BELOWPractical responsesVolume of cuttlebone / cm³Average titre / cm³Moles of HCl reacted with cuttlebone / molDensity of cuttlebone / g/cm³

L6 PracticalMOHR CRISPSYou are trying to work out just how salty your crisps are. Luckily there's a cunning titration for that, invented by this guy →You may only use the equipment provided at your experimental station.You may ask for experimental help at any time in the practical.1. Open your bag of crisps and transfer to your big beaker. (Try not to crush them as the crisp dust will cause all sorts of headaches down the line...)2. Using distilled water, dissolve all the salt. (Do not use more than 80 cm³ of water, and be aware crisps go pretty soggy if left soaking...)3. Add solution to a volumetric flask (filter on the way in to remove any excess crisp debris)4. Fill your burette with 0.1 mol dm⁻³ AgNO₃.5. Fill the volumetric flask up to the mark with distilled water.6. To a 250 cm³ conical flask add 40 cm³ of water, 20 cm³ of your salt solution and 2 cm³ of potassium chromate.7. Upon titration Ag⁺ will form a white precipitate with the chloride ions present. You’ll gradually see this. When all of the Cl⁻ has been used up, it will react with the CrO₄²⁻ to form silver chromate, which is a distinctive red-brown colour.8. Repeat for concordant titres. RECORD YOUR AVERAGE TITRE BELOW9. Find the mass of salt in a bag of crisps. RECORD THIS MASS BELOWPractical responsesAverage titre / cm³Mass of salt in bag of crisps / g

U6 PracticalCLIPPYYou are trying to work out what percentage of a paperclip is manganese, Mn. Follow the instructions below.You may only use the equipment provided at your experimental station.You may ask for experimental help at any time in the practical.1. Accurately weigh about 0.2 g of paperclip, you can cut pieces up to get this approximate mass. RECORD THIS BELOW2. Add the paperclip to 70 cm³ of 2 M nitric acid and take it to the fume cupboard. Gently warm. (the teacher may add some extra acid to help the paperclip dissolve).3. Use a pipette to add 10 cm³ of 85% H₃PO₄ and 10 cm³ of 0.217M KIO₄ (potassium periodate(VII)) and boil for 10 minutes. (This will oxidise the Mn in the paperclip into MnO₄⁻ via a series of pretty colours.)4. While this is reacting you will need to make a calibration curve by determining the absorbance of different concentration solutions of MnO₄⁻. To do this, first make a 0.0005 mol dm⁻³ solution of KMnO₄ mol dm⁻³ by dissolving solid KMnO₄ in 1M H₂SO₄(you may wish to make a more concentrated solution and then dilute it using the volumetric flasks provided.)5. You need to dilute this solution further to make a range of differing concentrations.6. Once you have at least 5 solutions with a range of concentrations (with 0.0005 mol dm⁻³  being the highest) you need to use the colorimeter to record the absorbance of these solutions.7. To use the colorimeter turn it on, then using the RGB button set the light to green, using the A/T button set the colorimeter to absorbance (A). Then add a cuvette of water and press CAL, the reading on the screen should be .0008. You are now ready to add your samples, which also need to be transferred to cuvettes, no buttons need to be pressed, just add the sample, close the lid and record the absorbance.9. You will need to plot a graph of absorbance against concentration, this is a calibration curve that will be used to find the concentration of your unknown solution made from the paperclip.10. Take your cooled beaker from the fume cupboard, transfer all of the solution to a 100 cm³ volumetric flask and make it up to the mark with distilled water.11. Invert to ensure a homogeneous solution and then add a sample to the cuvette, recording the absorbance. RECORD THIS BELOW12. Using your calibration curve find the concentration of your solution of MnO₄⁻ RECORD THIS BELOW13. Finally, find the mass of Mn in the paperclip and the percentage by mass that is Mn. RECORD THIS BELOWPractical responsesMass of paperclip / gAbsorbance of MnO₄⁻ from paperclipConcentration of MnO₄⁻ / mol dm⁻³Percentage of paperclip's mass that is Mn / %
